verdict.rationale: The separation at issue is the demerger of the Commercial Vehicles business out of the old Tata Motors Limited into TML Commercial Vehicles Limited, executed together with the amalgamation of the PV subsidiary back into the listed parent, under one Composite Scheme of Arrangement sanctioned by NCLT Mumbai (orders of August 25, 2025 and a rectification order of September 10, 2025), with an appointed date of July 1, 2025 and effective date of October 1, 2025. The Scheme states only two objectives in these texts: to transfer the Commercial Vehicles undertaking to the Resulting Company 'on a going concern basis' in compliance with Section 2(19AA) of the Income-tax Act, and to amalgamate Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited into TML 'with an objective of consolidating the Passenger Vehicles Business with TML', after which TML was renamed Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited and TMLCVL renamed Tata Motors Limited (w.e.f. October 13, 2025). The result is that, as the postal ballot puts it, 'the Commercial Vehicle and Passenger Vehicle businesses of the Company are housed in two separate entities', each with its own reconstituted board and KMP (Shailesh Chandra as MD & CEO of TMPV from October 1, 2025; P B Balaji moved from Group CFO to CEO of Jaguar Land Rover from November 17, 2025), and TMPV left reporting one automotive segment of JLR plus Tata Passenger Vehicles, 'other than CV segment moving out'. Shareholders were handed direct ownership of both: 1 TMLCVL share for every 1 TML share held on the October 14, 2025 record date, with historical cost apportioned 31.15% to the CV entity and 68.85% to TMPV, and the new CV shares listed from November 12, 2025. Management's only economic framing on the calls is accounting and capital: a notional demerger gain of ~Rs. 83,000 Cr (CV business valued at ~Rs. 94,000 Cr by third-party agencies against ~Rs. 11,000 Cr book value of net assets transferred), fully offset by a contra deemed-dividend entry so there is 'absolutely no impact on either distributable reserves or on our net worth'; an India PV business that is net cash (~Rs. 5,000 Cr at Q3 FY26, ~Rs. 7,000 Cr at FY26-end) which 'gives a lot of flex to fund the rich product investment cycle'; and the two entities now declaring dividends separately (Rs. 3 at TMPV plus Rs. 4 at TMLCV, 'a total dividend of Rs. 7 in the year when the demerger was undertaken' versus Rs. 6 before). Costs disclosed are stamp duty: a Rs. 400 Cr provision in Q3 FY26, included within about Rs. 4,100 Cr of FY26 exceptionals. No investor, lender or partner is named anywhere in these texts as having asked for the separation; the only stakeholder input recorded is the shareholder vote, which management described as 'overwhelming votes in our favor', and the nine AGM resolutions passed in July 2026.
verdict.evolution: On the Feb 2025 call (Q3 FY25, January 29, 2025) the demerger was already a filed corporate action awaiting exchange/SEBI NOC, with appointed date July 1 and effective date around October 1, 2025; by the Jun 2025 call (Q4 FY25, May 13, 2025) the shareholder vote had passed overwhelmingly and both dates were reconfirmed, and on the Aug 2025 call (Q1 FY26, August 8, 2025) the NCLT final hearing had concluded that same day with judgment reserved and the October 1 effective date 'on plan'. The Nov 2025 call (Q2 FY26, November 14, 2025) was the first set of results reported post-separation, where management walked through the demerger accounting entries, the Rs. 83,000 Cr notional gain and contra deemed dividend, and the new segment structure. Thereafter the subject narrows to residuals and costs: the Feb 2026 call (February 5, 2026) notes CV is out of the segments and books a Rs. 400 Cr stamp duty provision, and the Jun 2026 call (May 14, 2026) folds stamp duty into FY26 exceptionals and frames the two separate dividends as Rs. 7 combined; the strategic 'why' is never revisited on any of these six calls.

points.point: The Scheme bundles two steps: hiving off the Commercial Vehicles undertaking into TMLCVL on a going concern basis (structured to qualify under Section 2(19AA) of the Income-tax Act), and amalgamating the PV subsidiary into the listed parent — the only explicit objective language in any document supplied.
points.quote: Amalgamation of TMLPV with TML with an objective of consolidating the Passenger Vehicles Business with TML and consequent dissolution of TMLPV without being wound up.

points.point: The November 2025 postal ballot explains the consequence the separation was meant to produce — two self-standing entities — and uses it as the reason to rebuild both boards, appointing Shailesh Chandra MD & CEO of TMPV from October 1, 2025 and P B Balaji as a non-executive director while he became CEO of Jaguar Land Rover from November 17, 2025.
points.quote: In view of the above, it was proposed to reconstitute the Board of Directors of both  the entities .

points.point: Shareholders were given direct ownership of both businesses rather than cash, at a strict 1:1 entitlement on the October 14, 2025 record date, with historical cost of acquisition apportioned 31.15% to the CV entity and 68.85% to TMPV; the CV shares were approved for listing and trading from November 12, 2025.
points.quote: 1 (one) share of the Resulting Company (face value of INR 2/- each fully paid up), for every 1 (one) share of the Demerged Company (face value of INR 2/- each fully paid up) of the same class of shares outstanding and as held by such shareholder in the Demerged Company, without any further application, act or deed (‘Share Entitlement Ratio’).

points.point: At the 81st AGM (July 8, 2026) the Chairman and the MD & CEO presented the demerger as completed and as the platform for TMPV's own roadmap, pairing it with JLR's new Panapakkam, Tamil Nadu production and with long-term growth aspirations to FY31 on a consolidated basis.
points.quote: He highlighted the demerger of Commercial Vehicles business into a separate legal entity and commencement of commercial production by JLR at Panapakkam, Tamil Nadu reflecting the synergy between the Company and JLR.

points.point: The demerger was presented purely as a corporate action on track — filings with the exchanges and SEBI complete, operational carve-out work advanced, appointed date July 1 and effective date around October 1, 2025 — alongside the parallel Tata Motors Finance merger into Tata Capital.
points.quote: Operational activities are in an advanced stage and progressing as per plan.

points.point: Management reported that shareholders had backed the Scheme decisively and that both the appointed and effective dates were intact; asked about asset allocation, Balaji confirmed the Tata Capital stake would sit with the CV business after separation.
points.quote: we had overwhelming votes in our favor and therefore we are on track for an appointed date of July 1st

points.point: The NCLT final hearing concluded on the day of the call with judgment reserved, which management said would let them complete the demerger within the quarter for an October 1 effective date; the same slide carried the CV side's Iveco acquisition, i.e. each business already pursuing its own agenda.
points.quote: Hot of the press is the demerger.

points.point: First results after separation: the demerger produced a ~Rs. 83,000 Cr book gain on disposal of the CV undertaking (CV valued at ~Rs. 94,000 Cr by third-party agencies versus ~Rs. 11,000 Cr book value of net assets transferred), but it is entirely notional with no effect on net worth or distributable reserves.
points.quote: But this is only a notional gain as there is a contra entry of ~Rs. 83,000 Cr as a deemed dividend.

points.point: Reporting was simplified to one automotive segment comprising JLR and Tata Passenger Vehicles plus 'others' (mainly Tata Technologies and Tata Motors Holdings Pte Singapore); prior-period income statements were restated to TMPV only, while prior balance sheets still include CV and are not comparable.
points.quote: The automotive segment will now comprise of JLR and Tata Passenger Vehicles business.

points.point: Capital framing of the standalone PV entity: the India business is net cash, which management said gives flexibility to fund its heavy product investment cycle; one residual link to CV remains — the Rs. 6,500 Cr PLI cap still applies to PV and CV together because the original 2021 application was made as a Group.
points.quote: We had applied originally in 2021 as a Group.

points.point: CV is confirmed out of the reporting perimeter with nothing else changed, and the first demerger cost is booked — a Rs. 400 Cr stamp duty provision within Rs. 1,600 Cr of quarterly exceptionals alongside JLR cyber and India wage-bill charges.
points.quote: Commercial vehicle business is out I think last quarter post the demerger , everything else is the same.

points.point: FY26 exceptionals of about Rs. 4,100 Cr include demerger stamp duty; separately, the two entities now set dividends independently — Rs. 3 per share at TMPV (about Rs. 1,100 Cr outflow) plus Rs. 4 at TMLCV — which management framed as more total distribution than the pre-demerger company paid.
points.quote: So this actually represents a total dividend of Rs. 7 in the year when the demerger was undertaken and an increase over the Rs. 6 that we have paid for the last two years.

verdict.what_management_expects: Stated only indirectly: CV and PV housed in two separate listed entities, each with its own board, leadership and dividend (Rs. 3 + Rs. 4 vs Rs. 6 before); TMPV consolidating PV, EV and JLR under one automotive segment, with a net-cash India business (Rs. 7,000 Cr) giving flexibility to fund its product investment cycle while JLR carries Rs. 33,000 Cr net debt.
verdict.gaps: No value-unlock, focus, valuation or synergy argument; no demerger costs/benefits beyond stamp duty; no dis-synergies, debt-allocation logic, or any investor, lender or partner request.

verdict.rationale: Across the three transcripts tagged here (the Q3/9M FY26 call of February 10, 2026, which appears twice, and the Q4/FY26 call of May 21, 2026) and all 27 filings, Embassy Developments Limited (EMBDL/EDL) never announces, proposes or explains a separation, demerger, spin-off or carve-out of any of its own businesses — the stated direction of travel is the opposite, consolidation: FY26 was 'the first full year of the merged platform following the integration of NAM Estates and the erstwhile Indiabulls Real Estate Limited under the unified Embassy Developments brand', accounted for as a reverse merger under Ind AS 103 with NAM as accounting acquirer and EDL as accounting acquiree. The only separation management actually explains is historical and belongs to the predecessor group: a court-approved demerger in FY2010-11 that separated the power business, Sinnar Thermal Power Limited (STPL), from the erstwhile Indiabulls Group / real estate business, after which STPL was controlled by the unrelated Rattan India Group (Rattan India Power Limited and Rattan India Enterprises Limited) and 'was not under the control of the Company'. Management raised that 15-year-old separation only because a lender used its surviving guarantee framework against EDL: Canara Bank (successor to Syndicate Bank, which had sanctioned facilities aggregating Rs 1,444.00 million to STPL) claimed Rs 372 crore under a 2010/2011 corporate guarantee tied to an equity-infusion undertaking and filed a Section 7 IBC application; NCLT admitted CIRP on December 9, 2025, NCLAT stayed it on December 11, 2025, and on May 4, 2026 NCLAT quashed it, holding 'that no deed of guarantee existed and that the application was barred under Section 10A of the IBC', after which EDL exited the NSE ASM framework on May 6, 2026. EDL's defence rested on the separation itself: the obligation was an equity infusion and not 'debt', it was limited, contingent and secondary to the Rattan India Group post-demerger, and against a required infusion of Rs 2,454 crore the Rattan India Group had already infused Rs 3,026 crore, so no obligation survived. The forward-looking corporate actions in the window are consolidations and disposals rather than business separations: the Spero Properties and Services amalgamation into Equinox India Infraestate (appointed date April 1, 2025), and repeated voluntary strike-offs of non-operational subsidiaries (Ariston Investments, Lenus Constructions, Sentia Constructions, Equinox India Multiplex Services, Mariana Constructions, Apesh Real Estate, Varali Real Estate, Devona Infrastructure, Dev Property Development) undertaken 'to simplify its corporate structure and reduce administrative and compliance costs'. The closest thing to separating a business is asset-level monetisation: the April 11, 2026 share purchase agreement to sell 100% of Sepset Real Estate Limited — owner of the 'Mega Mall' commercial project in Jodhpur, which contributed Rs 18.55 crore of income (0.85%) and negative net worth of Rs 114.07 crore — to Pen India Limited for Rs 100 crore cash, plus the flagged disposal of non-core, non-contiguous Panvel parcels, possible disposal of the 500+ acre Sohna land where only ~75 acres is developable, and the Nashik 'debonding' exercise to strip SEZ status from ~1,500 acres so it can be sold as industrial plots. One potential separation was explicitly considered and dropped: management 'had a thought about forward purchasing' Embassy East Business Park (Phase 1, 2.7 msf, GDV ~Rs 3,100 crore) with Embassy REIT and chose instead to build it out and defer any exit-versus-hold decision by three to four years, while targeting an 80:20 residential:commercial mix moving toward 70:30. No investor, lender, banker or partner in these texts asks for a separation; the asks are presales and collections delivery, a lower cost of debt (14.8% down toward 10%), lower leverage (0.3x net debt/equity), reduction of the promoter pledge (68% back toward 47-48%), and clarity on when the reported P&L turns positive.
verdict.evolution: February 10, 2026 (Q3/9M FY26, the first earnings call as the merged entity): the only separation discussed is the FY2010-11 court-approved demerger of the power business (STPL) from the erstwhile Indiabulls Group, surfaced purely as context for Canara Bank's Rs 372 crore Section 7 claim and the NCLAT stay, while a possible REIT carve-out of Embassy East Business Park is disclosed as considered and dropped in favour of building it out. Between calls the separation-adjacent activity is disposal, not demerger: the April 11-12, 2026 sale of Sepset Real Estate (Mega Mall, Jodhpur) to Pen India for Rs 100 crore, continuing subsidiary strike-offs (March 10/16, April 6/21, June 10, 2026), and the May 4, 2026 NCLAT order quashing CIRP on the merits of the old demerger-era guarantee. May 21, 2026 (Q4/FY26): the legacy separation is closed out as a won litigation, and management reframes portfolio pruning — monetising scattered/unmutated erstwhile-Indiabulls land, entertaining offers on Sohna, and 'debonding' the ~1,500-acre Nashik SEZ — as non-core exits rather than any business separation. Nothing in the August-October 2026 filings (Rs 1,020 crore and Rs 105 crore NCDs, the Rs 362.62 crore promoter warrant issue fully converted by October 30, 2026) introduces a separation; they raise and recapitalise within one entity.

points.point: The only separation management explains is the FY2010-11 court-approved demerger that moved the power business (Sinnar Thermal Power Limited) out of the erstwhile Indiabulls Group, raised solely as background to the insolvency case.
points.quote: The case relates to facilities availed by Sinnar Thermal Power Limited, in 2011 following a court-approved demerger under which the power business was separated from the erstwhile Indiabulls Group and certain historical corporate guarantee arrangements linked to equity infusion obligations.

points.point: Post-separation ownership of STPL moved to the unrelated Ratan/Rattan India Group, which is the factual basis for EDL denying liability; the lender nonetheless claimed Rs 372 crore under the old guarantee framework.
points.quote: Canara Bank has initiated proceedings against the company alleging liability for repayment of loans of Rs. 372 crore under an erstwhile corporate guarantee framework and filed a Section 7 application under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016.

points.point: The Q3 FY26 investor update (filed February 9, 2026) frames the 2010-11 demerger as a reorganisation that split power from real estate, and states Rattan India infused Rs 3,026 crore against a required Rs 2,454 crore, so no equity-infusion obligation survives on EDL.
points.quote: In FY 2010-11, a court-approved demerger reorganised the group's businesses, pursuant to which the power business was separated from the real estate business.

points.point: NCLAT decided the demerger-era guarantee question on the merits on May 4, 2026, quashing the CIRP entirely and letting EDL exit the ASM framework and resume normal trading from May 6, 2026.
points.quote: The NCLAT held inter alia that no deed of guarantee existed and that the application was barred under Section 10A of the IBC.

points.point: The only business actually detached from EDL in the period is the Jodhpur 'Mega Mall' commercial project, via sale of 100% of Sepset Real Estate Limited to Pen India Limited for Rs 100 crore cash under an agreement dated April 11, 2026 — framed as portfolio pruning and capital redeployment, not a demerger.
points.quote: The monetisation of this asset will unlock value and strengthen the Company's balance sheet, while enabling redeployment of capital in to core markets and high-growth opportunities.

points.point: A possible separation of the commercial asset into Embassy REIT was considered and rejected for now: EDL will build out Embassy East Business Park Phase 1 (2.7 msf, GDV ~Rs 3,100 crore) and decide on an exit or hold only near completion, three to four years out.
points.quote: We had a thought about forward purchasing it with Embassy REIT. We have decided now to just build it out.

points.point: Instead of separating a business, management plans asset-level exits of inherited non-core land — scattered or unaggregated erstwhile-Indiabulls parcels, the 500+ acre Sohna holding where only ~75 acres is developable, and non-contiguous Panvel parcels.
points.quote: And wherever we have land parcels which are not mutated or scattered or the aggregation was not done by the erstwhile Indiabulls, we are definitely looking at monetizing that.

points.point: The ~1,500-acre Nashik holding is being 'debonded' — separating its SEZ status rather than the business — so it can be sold as small and mid-market industrial plots once the MIDC dispute is settled.
points.quote: So converting the land from SEZ to not having an SEZ status out here.

points.point: The structural work disclosed in filings runs toward fewer entities, not a separation: the Spero Properties amalgamation into Equinox India Infraestate and a string of voluntary subsidiary strike-offs.
points.quote: as part of the Company's ongoing initiative to simplify its corporate structure and reduce administrative and compliance costs

points.point: Management's own strategic framing is consolidation of two platforms into one listed developer with ~38 msf and a 3,100+ acre land bank across 8 cities — the stated rationale is scale and access, the inverse of a separation thesis.
points.quote: This merger was not simply about consolidation. It was a deliberate step to create a stronger, more resilient and future ready listed real estate platform, one with institutional scale, deeper operating capabilities and broader access to high quality markets.

verdict.what_management_expects: No separation benefits are claimed, because none is planned. For the disposals they do describe: unlocked value, a stronger balance sheet and capital redeployed into core markets; non-core land exits and Nashik debonding to raise realisable value; lower cost of debt (14.8% toward 10%) and net debt/equity near 0.3x; ~47-50% net cash surplus margins; simpler structure cutting compliance cost.
verdict.gaps: The premise: these texts contain no EMBDL separation, demerger or spin-off — no rationale, structure, record date, entity split, valuation, lender consent, or investor/partner demand for one.

verdict.rationale: Read against the documents, HSCL is not separating a business of its own — it is the receiving side of a separation: the 21 September 2026 Scheme demerges the Tyre Business (Birla Tyres, Balasore) out of Dalmia Bharat Refractories Limited (DBRL, the Demerged Company) and vests it in HSCL (the Resulting Company) as a going concern on an as-is-where-is basis with appointed date 1 October 2026, with no cash consideration — only 1 new HSCL share of Re 1 for every 260 DBRL shares of Rs 10, which adds just 1,76,462 shares and moves promoter holding from 52.49% to 52.47% (50,45,74,175 to 50,47,50,637 shares). The Board's stated reasons are: strategic forward integration of tyres with HSCL's existing carbon black and advanced carbon materials business; leveraging HSCL's material expertise, R&D, manufacturing and customer relationships for tyre product customisation; synergies across raw material sourcing, product development, manufacturing, logistics, distribution, market development, shared services and customer engagement; direct ownership and control to coordinate capacity utilisation, modernisation and product expansion; and greater strategic and financial flexibility to align investment, funding and capacity expansion — plus 'more focused ownership and a robust operating structure' so each company can direct management attention and capital to its own strengths. The business being moved is small and loss-making for now: turnover of the Demerged Undertaking was INR 149.31 crores at 31 March 2026, just 3.39% of HSCL's turnover (management separately cited Birla Tyres FY26 topline of INR 187 crores, INR 60+ crores in Q3FY26, INR 26 crores in Q2FY26, INR 5 crores in Q1FY26 and INR 127 crores in Q1FY27), with commercial operations only from 29 May 2025, EBITDA breakeven/cash-positive guided 'in this financial year' (FY27), and a target of INR 3,000 crores topline in 4-5 years. The problem it solves, as the calls make plain, is the awkward interim structure: tyres were manufactured on DBRL's balance sheet and merely bought and resold by wholly-owned Himadri Clean Energy, so HSCL booked tyre revenue but no tyre profit — 'we don't have any positive or negative impact as such as of now' (Jan 2026), 'we have not consolidated' (Apr 2026), and 'once it becomes part of Himadri, then the numbers will come' (Jul 2026). Direct ownership also lines up with the heavy spend already running through tyres — roughly INR 250-300 crores of additional capex in FY26 continuing for three years, and INR 500 crores of the ~INR 2,000 crores FY27-28 capex earmarked for Birla Tyres to convert Truck & Bus Bias capacity to OTR/OHT and commission a PCR line by FY28 for EV/SUV tyres. Notably, nobody on these calls says investors, lenders or partners demanded the step: analysts repeatedly pushed for tyre consolidation and segment numbers (Sanjesh Jain, Jul 2025; Dhruvin Kadakia, Apr 2026; Bhavin Chheda, Jul 2026) and Bharat Shah of ASK questioned whether a B2C tyre business was a distraction from speciality chemicals, but the Scheme is presented purely as a Board decision backed by a valuation report and a fairness opinion, with no lender or JV-partner request disclosed.
verdict.evolution: Through FY26 management framed Birla Tyres as deliberately arm's-length: on the Jul 18, 2025 call it was 'a standalone business' with its own P&L, HSCL explicitly selling it no carbon black, and when asked when the manufacturing entity would come inside HSCL the answer was flat — 'there is no intention as such now as of date.' The Oct 24, 2025 and Jan 21, 2026 calls kept the trading structure (Himadri Clean Energy buying from DBRL and reselling, so tyre margin landed nowhere in HSCL), while distributors grew 20 → 29 → 36; by Apr 27, 2026 the line was 'we have not consolidated — once we consolidate, then we can discuss this,' and on Jul 16, 2026 the CMD said tyres still sit on Dalmia Refractory's balance sheet and 'once it becomes part of Himadri, then the numbers will come,' alongside a INR 500 crore tyre capex plan. The Board then gave notice on 18 September 2026 and approved the demerger Scheme on 21 September 2026 (valuation and fairness opinion both dated 20 September 2026), with 1 October 2026 as the appointed date.

points.point: At the outset the tyre entry was positioned as deliberately non-integrated: Himadri would not supply carbon black to Birla Tyres because it could sell the same black at a premium elsewhere, and each business kept its own P&L.
points.quote: However, it is important to note that Himadri will not be selling any carbon black to Birla Tyres.

points.point: Asked directly when the tyre manufacturing entity would be brought inside Himadri, management ruled it out at the time, calling Birla Tyres a standalone business acquired for about INR 300 crores against assets worth INR 3,400 crores.
points.quote: No, there is no intention as such now as of date of its coming into Himadri.

points.point: Bharat Shah of ASK Investment Managers challenged the fit of a B2C tyre business inside a B2B speciality chemicals company; the CMD defended it as the ready-made launching pad into B2C with a 40-year brand, run by a separate vertical head.
points.quote: See, today or tomorrow I have to go into B2C.

points.point: Six months into operations tyre sales were immaterial (INR 26 crores in Q2FY26 against INR 5 crores in Q1FY26), with 29 distributors and over 350 dealers and the year treated as a start-up phase.
points.quote: So, this year is like a start-up. To be very frank, we are not considering this as any revenue.

points.point: The interim structure was spelled out: tyres were made under the Dalmia Bharat Refractories partnership and merely bought and resold by Himadri Clean Energy, so no tyre profit or loss reached HSCL on INR 60+ crores of quarterly tyre revenue.
points.quote: So in Himadri, in Himadri Clean Energy, we are buying from Dalmia Refractory and selling the Birla Tyres. So we don't have any positive or negative impact as such as of now.

points.point: Asked for tyre volumes and realisation, management refused on the ground that tyres were not consolidated — only clubbed into an 'others' segment with mining — while disclosing FY26 tyre topline of INR 187 crores and a INR 3,000 crore ambition in four years.
points.quote: Tyre still now, we have not consolidated. Once we consolidate, then we can discuss this.

points.point: On Bhavin Chheda's question whether the INR 127 crore quarterly tyre revenue was EBITDA positive, the CMD said not yet and tied the missing profit disclosure explicitly to the business sitting on DBRL's balance sheet pending transfer into Himadri.
points.quote: So now Birla Tyres is reflected on Dalmia Refractory balance sheet. So once it becomes part of Himadri, then the numbers will come.

points.point: The capital case for direct ownership: INR 500 crores of the ~INR 2,000 crore FY27-FY28 capex is for Birla Tyres, funding phased TBB-to-OTR conversion, modernisation/automation, 400+ new SKUs and a PCR line by FY28, with breakeven guided for FY27.
points.quote: We reach EBITDA breakeven in this financial year only. We will be cash positive.

points.point: The Board's first stated benefit is forward integration — folding the tyre business into HSCL's carbon black and advanced carbon materials platform to own more of the tyre value chain, reversing the earlier 'separate P&Ls, no internal carbon black sales' stance.
points.quote: The Demerger will enable the Resulting Company to integrate the Tyre Business with its existing carbon black and advanced carbon materials business, thereby strengthening its presence across the tyre value chain.

points.point: Control and funding flexibility are cited as the operating rationale: direct ownership lets HSCL coordinate capacity utilisation, modernisation, product expansion and distribution, and align tyre investment and funding with group strategy.
points.quote: Direct ownership will enable the Resulting Company to align investment, funding, capacity expansion and growth priorities of the Tyre Business with its broader business strategy.

points.point: Scale of what moves: the Demerged Undertaking (all assets, liabilities, contracts, employees, brands, trademarks, licences of DBRL's tyre business) had turnover of INR 149.31 crores at 31 March 2026, only 3.39% of HSCL's turnover.
points.quote: Turnover of the Demerged Undertaking as on 31 March 2026, was INR 149.31 crores, which constitutes 3.39% of total turnover of Resulting Company in the immediately preceding financial year / based on financials of last financial year (i.e. for year ended 31 March 2026).

points.point: Consideration is non-cash and barely dilutive: 1 HSCL share per 260 DBRL shares, based on a 20 September 2026 valuation by SSPA & Co and CA Manish Gadia with a fairness opinion from Jajodia Equity Advisors; promoter holding moves 52.49% to 52.47%.
points.quote: 1 (One) fully paid-up equity shares of face value of INR 1 (one) each of the Resulting Company shall be issued and allotted for every 260 (Two Hundred Sixty) fully paid-up equity shares of face value of INR 10 (ten) each held in the Demerged Company

points.point: The Board also frames it as cleaner ownership for both sides, letting DBRL and HSCL each direct management attention, capital and resources to businesses matching their own strategic capabilities.
points.quote: the proposed Demerger would provide a more focused ownership and robust operating structure for the Demerged Undertaking, while enabling each of the Companies to deploy its management attention, capital and resources towards businesses aligned with its respective strategic capabilities and long-term objectives.

verdict.what_management_expects: For HSCL: forward integration across the tyre value chain, synergies in sourcing, product development, logistics, distribution and shared services, direct control over capacity utilisation, modernisation, OTR/PCR expansion, and flexibility to fund it — tyres reaching EBITDA breakeven in FY27 and INR 3,000 crores topline in 4-5 years. For DBRL: focused ownership, with management attention and capital redirected to its own strategic businesses.
verdict.gaps: No reason given for DBRL exiting or for reversing the Jul 2025 'no intention' stance; no tyre EBITDA, debt, or treatment of HSCL's INR 300 crore stake, NCDs or HBTMPL 49%.

verdict.segment_name: Tyres Business (Birla Tyres Limited / Himadri Birla Tyre Manufacturer Private Limited) — described in the annual report as "OUR TYRES BUSINESS" under Business Segment Analysis, but not a reportable segment in HSCL's segment note
verdict.unit: ₹ lakhs (unit used in the consolidated segment note); presentations use ₹ crore
verdict.measure_notes: No profit or revenue line exists for the tyre business anywhere on these pages. HSCL's consolidated segment note reports only 'Carbon materials and chemicals', 'Power' and (FY2026 only) 'Others — Mining and Other business'; 'Segment results' there are earnings before other income, finance cost, FX gain/(loss) and tax, with revenue split into external and inter-segment. The FY2026 'Others' segment (external revenue 27,446.09 lakhs, segment result 2,780.71 lakhs) is labelled Mining and Other business and is NOT identified as the tyre business, so it has not been used. Presentation figures (FY26 revenue ₹4,660.7 Cr, EBITDA ₹1,006 Cr, PBT ₹1,001 Cr, PAT ₹755 Cr consolidated; Q1FY26 standalone revenue ₹1,200 Cr, EBITDA ₹234 Cr, PAT ₹183 Cr) are whole-company, not tyre-business.

Annual Report 2025 — page 433 (segment note lists only Carbon materials and chemicals, Power; no tyre segment)

verdict.not_found: No tyre-business revenue, EBITDA/segment result or PAT on any page — annual or quarterly. Pages carry only qualitative tyre commentary, capex (₹306 Cr) and Q1FY26 commencement timing.

verdict.rationale: Management framed the demerger as splitting one company that had been doing two businesses with two different investor bases: an asset-heavy business that designs, develops, finances and owns hotels (pension funds, insurance companies betting on inflation, repricing and annuity yield) and an asset-light business that monetises brand, management, loyalty, distribution and technology with almost no capital intensity. Keswani said Lemon Tree had only built hotels in 2004-2007 because owners would not hand their hotels to an unknown brand, and that with the brand now widely recognised (MakeMyTrip's CEO told him 20-25% of occupancy comes from them the moment a Lemon Tree opens) there was no reason to keep owning assets rather than monetise the brand — explicitly the Marriott/Host Hotels and Hilton/Park Hotels playbook. Mechanically (Composite Scheme approved 9 Jan 2026, appointed date 1 April 2026): Carnation Hotels and Hamstede Living merge into LTH; Oriole Dr. Fresh, Canary, Sukhsagar and Manakin merge into Fleur against shares to LTH; and the Demerged Undertaking — 11 operating hotels plus Aurika Shimla under construction, the investment in Arum (Aurika Shillong, 165 rooms) and the entire development capability/team with exclusivity on all future ownership, leasing and development — demerges into Fleur, with 20 Fleur shares for every 311 LTH shares (demerged division turnover Rs 23,037.34 lakh, 59.90% of LTH standalone turnover; 1,563 operating rooms across 15 hotels per the presentation, 1,820 keys/17 hotels per the press release). A second stated problem was conflict of interest: development capability was moved to Fleur with 'Chinese firewalls' so Fleur shareholders could never feel Lemon Tree was cherry-picking the best assets for itself, and Lemon Tree must refer new acquisition/development opportunities to Fleur. All group debt (about Rs 1,300 crore at demerger, Rs 1,500 crore total borrowings at FY26-end, cost of debt 7.42%) goes to Fleur, leaving Lemon Tree debt-free with only technology and marketing spend, forcing the Board to frame a dividend/shareholder-reward policy. Warburg Pincus (Coastal Cedar Investments B.V.) bought APG's entire 41.09% of Fleur and committed up to Rs 960 crore of primary equity, giving Fleur roughly Rs 3,000 crore of deployable capital at 1:1 debt-equity against 2,500+ rooms under active discussion and Aurika Nehru Place (572 rooms, ~Rs 700 crore); post-scheme LTH shareholders own ~74% of Fleur (32.96% direct plus ~41% through LTH) versus the 59% LTH owns today, and Fleur lists separately for 'transparent price discovery and market-driven valuation of the asset-heavy business'.
verdict.evolution: The idea was first visible as a Fleur listing aspiration in the Nov 2024 call, where Keswani said debt-freedom would come sooner 'if we list Fleur before that' and put an IPO 'within the next 2-3 years at most'; in the Aug 2025 call he disclosed that committees of directors had been set up in both Lemon Tree and Fleur to evaluate transferring LTH's assets into Fleur via a demerger and listing it, alongside splitting the management teams (Neelendra Singh for LTH from 1 October, Saurabh Shatdal for Fleur), with listing hoped for end-CY2026. In the Nov 2025 call it was 'in process' with a Board subcommittee and a promise of 'some other even more exciting stuff' within three months; the scheme, the Warburg/APG transactions and the 74%/26% shareholding math were announced in the Jan 2026 (15 January) dedicated call with a 12-15 month path to listing. By the Feb 2026 call Keswani confirmed the scheme was effective from 1 April and, responding to Ashish Kumar's request, promised pro forma financials for both entities; those pro formas appeared with the Jun 2026 (29 May) results, where CCI approval (April 2026), Warburg's completed purchase of APG's stake and a longer 12-18 month NCLT-dependent timeline were given, followed by NSE/BSE observation letters on 22 September 2026.

points.point: Asked directly by Kunal Lakhan (CLSA) what was wrong with the old structure, Keswani said the hotel business has two subsets with two different investor types — developers/owners wanting chunky yield and inflation-linked annuity returns versus asset-light investors betting on brand and management — and Lemon Tree was a combination of both.
points.quote: We have actually separated 2 types of businesses. One is asset heavy, long -term appreciating asset, capital intensive. It has a different kind of investor, and this business has a very different kind of investor, and we wanted to actually attract both types of investors.

points.point: He explained the historical accident being corrected: hotels were built only to establish the brand, and with the brand now established the company should monetise it instead of owning assets.
points.quote: We were forced to build hotels to build our brand. But once we build our brand, technically, we do not need hotels because now it is time for Lemon Tree to monetize its brand, which is enormous recall.

points.point: The transfer of the development capability and exclusive development mandate to Fleur was driven by a conflict-of-interest problem — Fleur minorities fearing Lemon Tree would keep the best projects for itself — and was solved with firewalls.
points.quote: Development capability was an issue which was raised in order to maximize Fleur's growth, we did not want shareholders of Fleur to ever feel that Lemon Tree when it recommends any assets was cherry -picking, which means Lemon Tree would say, I have got this very nice asset in Delhi, why should I offer it to Fleur.

points.point: All of Lemon Tree's debt moves to Fleur: Fleur carries roughly Rs 1,300 crore of debt against a ~Rs 900 crore net EBITDA and can borrow another ~Rs 1,300 crore, while Lemon Tree goes to zero debt.
points.quote: Firstly, when this demerger happens, all the debt, including the Lemon Tree's debt, after adjustment is being transferred to Fleur. Fleur will have 100% of our debt and Lemon Tree will have zero debt.

points.point: Keswani justified keeping a ~41% indirect stake in Fleur (challenged by Jinesh Joshi on hold-co discount) as Lemon Tree retaining 'skin in the game' as Fleur's manager, with natural dilution as Fleur raises capital; he quantified that Rs 1,000 crore deployed by Fleur generates ~Rs 350 crore of turnover, Rs 170-180 crore EBITDA and ~Rs 30 crore of fees for Lemon Tree.
points.quote: We felt it was prudent to have significant skin in the game at this stage, which means that going forward, it is very possible that Lemon Tree may dilute or even increase its stake over time; this will obviously be a Board decision .

points.point: Warburg's Rs 960 crore primary commitment plus Fleur's own cash and 1:1 debt gives roughly Rs 3,000 crore to deploy pre-listing against 2,500 rooms in active discussion; Keswani guided Fleur to over Rs 1,000 crore net EBITDA by FY28 and Lemon Tree to 80% EBITDA margin / 60% PAT margin.
points.quote: We have potentially about Rs 3,000 crores available to deploy in this growth before we list.

points.point: Opening the call with pro forma financials for both entities, Keswani described the transaction as simple — Warburg has bought APG's Fleur stake, Lemon Tree transfers 17 hotels and development capabilities in exchange for Fleur shares to LTH shareholders, and Fleur lists.
points.quote: This scheme will result in 2 distinct financially sound businesses.

points.point: He restated the economic outcome for each entity: Lemon Tree debt-free, high-margin, high-ROCE and fee/brand-driven; Fleur the consolidated owner of a fully renovated portfolio, post-scheme India's largest hotel platform by inventory at 5,600 rooms and 39 operational hotels.
points.quote: Post the reorganization , Lemon Tree will emerge as a debt -free, high-margin, high ROCE company generating strong free cash flows from fees and brand -related income.

points.point: Shareholder arithmetic: LTH shareholders end up with close to 74% of Fleur (33% direct, ~41% through Lemon Tree) versus the 59% Lemon Tree directly owns in Fleur today, before Warburg's primary infusion; Keswani also said he will cease to be executive at Lemon Tree from March 2027 and focus on Fleur as Executive Chair.
points.quote: Post reorganization , Lemon Tree shareholders will effectively own close to 74% of Fleur Hotels, 33% directly and about 41% indirectly through Lemon Tree.

points.point: Answering Achal Kumar, Keswani confirmed Fleur will be brand-agnostic post-demerger and may hand assets to other operators — Lemon Tree has no automatic right to Fleur's hotels and must earn them on results.
points.quote: Yes. But Lemon Tree must be able to deliver best results to get it . Just because Lemon Tree has skin in the game with Fleur does not mean that it has an automatic right to any asset that Fleur develops.

points.point: On capital allocation after the split, Lemon Tree is expected to need almost no capital and move to distributing profits, while Fleur will retain capital for growth rather than pay dividends.
points.quote: Lemon Tree will not need any significant capital other than potentially investments in technology or in marketing and so on. It will be essentially a zero -debt cash accretive company.

points.point: Keswani confirmed the scheme is effective from 1 April and that Lemon Tree becomes debt-free from next year, with all assets and debt going to Fleur and fee income becoming free cash; the Board must decide a dividend policy within six months.
points.quote: What will happen is in the scheme of demerger, all the assets of Lemon Tree, including its debt will be transferred to Fleur. Lemon Tree will immediately effectively be a debt -free company from next year.

points.point: Investors pushed for separate reporting: Ashish Kumar of Infinity Alternatives asked for pro forma financials of both businesses while awaiting the listing, and management agreed to publish them from the next quarter.
points.quote: Now that we have decided on the split of the 2 businesses, what might be helpful is if we can add pro forma financials for both of the assets as they look like so that while we are waiting for the l isting, we do get a good sense of what the numbers are looking like.

points.point: Keswani positioned the asset-light entity as a first in India, with fee income from hotels signed three years earlier only now flowing, and Fleur guided to ~Rs 1,000 crore EBITDA by FY28, its first year as a listed company.
points.quote: And keep in mind that Lemon Tree will be the first fully asset -light brand owning tech and distribution and management company in India, the first.

points.point: The demerger was still with Board subcommittees of both Lemon Tree and Fleur, with management hinting that more than the demerger was being negotiated (the Warburg/APG transactions announced two months later).
points.quote: It is not only the demerger of Fleur, but some other even more exciting stuff, but we will talk about it when the time is right.

points.point: First formal disclosure of the structure: committees of directors in both companies to evaluate transferring LTH's assets into Fleur via demerger and then list Fleur, with Lemon Tree becoming asset-light and focused on management, brand and technology — described as the global trend in the space.
points.quote: You may have also seen that we have said that a committee of directors has been set up in Lemon Tree and in Fleur to evaluate how we can possibly look at a transfer of assets from Lemon Tree into Fleur through a demerger scheme and then automatically look at how we can list Fleur.

points.point: The separation of management was done first and explicitly for this purpose — Neelendra Singh to run asset-light Lemon Tree from 1 October and Saurabh Shatdal to drive Fleur's asset-heavy growth, with Keswani handholding and moving to strategic oversight.
points.quote: The intent of the leadership change was to get 2 very good people who would then run these two companies independently on a day -to-day basis.

points.point: Keswani drew a hard line on mandates — Fleur builds, buys and leases, Lemon Tree only manages or franchises — and noted that the more Fleur dilutes and raises capital, the more Lemon Tree's economic interest rises via fees (Rs 100+ crore this year, potentially Rs 300-400 crore from Fleur in three years).
points.quote: Fleur's mandate will be to focus on, at the right value, building, buying, or leasing hotels. Lemon Tree's will only be to manage or franchise. Lemon Tree will not lease hotels once the Fleur demerger happens.

points.point: The earliest trace in these calls: a Fleur listing was already seen as the accelerator of deleveraging, with Keswani putting an IPO within 2-3 years at most when asked by Prashant Biyani.
points.quote: I think we are sticking to our guidance that in the next 3 - 3.5 years, we should be debt free , but if we list Fleur before that then we will be debt free that much earlier.

points.point: The 9 Jan 2026 filing states the Board reviewed the business with a view to segregating the asset-heavy ownership/development undertaking from the asset-light management/brand platform, and that the demerged business is self-sustaining and better housed in Fleur; the demerged division's turnover was Rs 23,037.34 lakh, 59.90% of LTH standalone turnover.
points.quote: Therefore, to achieve operational focus, greater flexibility for capital deployment, and clearer alignment of business objectives, it is proposed under this Scheme to (i) amalgamate Transferor Company 3, Transferor Company 4, Transferor Company 5 and Transferor Company 6 with the Transferee Company; and (ii) demerge and vest the Demerged Undertaking (comprising the Demerged Hotel Properties and the Development Capabilities together with the related undertakings, as defined hereinafter) into the Transferee C ompany, while the Company will continue to focus on the asset -light hotel management support, brand and operations including management support of the hotels transferred to the Transferee Company and other properties.

points.point: A stated purpose is market-driven valuation: Fleur ceases to be LTH's subsidiary and lists, so LTH shareholders participate directly in the asset-heavy business through listed shares rather than through a subsidiary.
points.quote: Following the implementation of the Scheme, the Transferee Company will cease to be a subsidiary of the Company , and its shares will be listed on the Stock Exchanges, enabling transparent price discovery and market -driven valuation of the asset -heavy business.

points.point: The filing also sets out structural clean-up and partner-flexibility objectives: merging two wholly owned subsidiaries into LTH to remove layering and cost, and creating a structure that lets Fleur bring in investors or co-development partners per project without touching LTH's brand operations.
points.quote: To create a flexible structure enabling the Transferee Company to attract investors or co -development partners for specific hotel projects, without affecting Company's brand operations or control over strategic decisions.

points.point: Continuity is contractually locked: every hotel amalgamated into or demerged to Fleur stays under Lemon Tree Hotel Operating Agreements (existing ones amended/restated and extended from the Appointed Date), and LTH must refer new acquisition/development opportunities to Fleur and drop them if Fleur declines.
points.quote: Further, all the hotels amalgamated with or demerged into the Transferee Company will continue to be managed and operated by the Company under Hotel Operating Agreements and, the existing Hotel Operating Agreements with the Transferee Company and its subsidiaries shall be amended and/or restated, inter alia, to reflect the revised terms as detailed in the Scheme, and the Company shall refer new hotel acquisition or development opportunities to the Transferee Company and shall not pursue them if declined, except for hotel operations/franchise arran gements through third parties.

points.point: The Shareholders' Agreement with Warburg gives Fleur the exclusive global right to own, lease and develop hospitality assets, Investor/LTH affirmative consent on reserved matters, up to 3 Investor and 3 LTH directors with Keswani as non-retiring executive chairman, and the right to inject up to Rs 960 crore of primary capital.
points.quote: The Agreement provides Fleur t he exclusive right to own, lease and develop hospitality assets globally, with LTHL being entitled to undertake key money arrangements, in the manner as mutually agreed.

points.point: The 22 Sept 2026 filing records receipt of NSE 'no objection' and BSE 'no adverse observation' letters under Regulation 37, valid six months, with NCLT, shareholder and creditor approvals still pending — the gating item management had flagged as the timing risk.
points.quote: In this regard, we wish to inform you that the Company has received the Observation Letter s with 'no objection ' from the NSE and 'no adverse observations' from the BSE on September 22, 2026 vide their respective letters , pursuant to Regulation 37 of the Listing Regulations , in relation to the Scheme .

verdict.what_management_expects: Lemon Tree: debt-free, fee/brand/tech-only, EBITDA margin from ~60% pro forma to 70-80% steady state, ~60% PAT margin, high ROCE, free cash funding dividends. Fleur: India's largest owner (5,600 rooms, 39 hotels), net EBITDA Rs 850 crore FY27 and Rs 1,000+ crore FY28, ~48%+ post-fee margins, Warburg-backed capital for 2,500+ rooms, capital growth not dividends, and separately listed for market valuation.
verdict.gaps: Absolute valuation of the demerged undertaking and Warburg's price for APG's stake, Fleur's issue price, hold-co discount size, post-demerger ROE, and fate of the two retained leases.
